questions.stem: ASSERTION (A): A passenger in a moving bus lurches forward when the bus brakes suddenly. REASON (R): Friction between the passenger's feet and the floor is transferred instantly to the passenger's upper body.

options.option_text: Both A and R are true, R is the correct explanation
A is true but R is false
A is false, R is true
Both A and R are false

questions.explanation: A is TRUE: the passenger lurches forward. R is FALSE: the real cause is the INERTIA (Newton's First Law) — the passenger's body tends to keep moving when the bus decelerates, so the body surges relative to the decelerated bus. Friction between feet and floor actually OPPOSES forward motion, not the other way. Classic A-true-R-false pattern.

questions.stem: A car of mass 1000 kg moving at 20 m/s collides head-on with a wall and stops in 0.5 s. Average force exerted on the wall is:
questions.explanation: Impulse–momentum: F·t = Δp. Δp = m·(v − u) = 1000 × (0 − 20) = −20,000 kg·m/s. F = Δp/Δt = 20,000/0.5 = 40,000 N = 40 kN (magnitude on the wall by Newton's third law).

questions.stem: A body is dropped from rest from a height of 45 m (g = 10 m/s²). The time it takes to hit the ground and the velocity on impact are:
questions.explanation: h = ½ g t² → 45 = 5 t² → t² = 9 → t = 3 s. v = g·t = 10 × 3 = 30 m/s. Alternatively v² = u² + 2 g h = 900 → v = 30.

questions.stem: Consider the following statements about WORK–ENERGY. 1. Work done by a centripetal force on a body in uniform circular motion is zero. 2. Kinetic energy is a vector quantity. 3. The work-energy theorem states that net work done equals the change in kinetic energy. 4. Gravitational potential energy depends on the choice of reference level. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement 2 is WRONG — KE = ½ m v² is a SCALAR. It has no direction. Statement 1 is correct because centripetal force is always perpendicular to velocity → W = F·d·cos 90° = 0. Statements 3 (work-energy theorem) and 4 (PE is relative to a chosen zero) are correct.

questions.stem: A 2 kg block is pulled along a rough horizontal surface by a horizontal force of 20 N. If the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.4 and g = 10 m/s², the block's acceleration is:
questions.explanation: Friction force f = μ·N = 0.4 × 2 × 10 = 8 N. Net horizontal force = 20 − 8 = 12 N. Acceleration a = F/m = 12/2 = 6 m/s².

questions.stem: A bullet of mass 10 g moving at 400 m/s embeds in a 2 kg block resting on a frictionless surface. The common velocity of the block + bullet immediately after impact is closest to:
questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum (perfectly inelastic): (0.01)(400) + (2)(0) = (2.01) v → v = 4/2.01 ≈ 1.99 m/s ≈ 2 m/s. KE is NOT conserved in inelastic collisions — momentum IS.

questions.stem: Which quantity is INVARIANT across Galilean frames of reference (at non-relativistic speeds)?
questions.explanation: In classical (Galilean) mechanics, time is ABSOLUTE — the same interval between two events is measured by all inertial observers. Velocity and KE and momentum all transform with frame-change. (In special relativity, even time is frame-dependent — but that's the whole point of Einstein's revision.)

questions.stem: If the escape velocity from Earth is 11.2 km/s, the escape velocity from a planet of the SAME density but TWICE the radius would be closest to:
questions.explanation: Escape velocity v_e = √(2GM/R). With constant density, M ∝ R³, so GM/R ∝ R². Hence v_e ∝ R. Doubling R doubles v_e → 22.4 km/s. Trap 15.8 comes from v_e ∝ √R (density not constant).
